source.title: EDA Built-in Knowledge: Power Conversion and Regulation

facts.text: A linear regulator (e.g. 1117, 2951 family) drops excess voltage across a pass transistor; the output is held at a fixed or set value. Efficiency is approximately Vout/Vin; the difference is dissipated as heat.

A linear regulator needs its input to be at least its dropout voltage above the output (often ~1 V for older parts, <300 mV for low-dropout parts); if the input collapses the output cannot be maintained.

A buck (step-down) converter uses a high-side switch (MOSFET), a synchronous or freewheeling low-side switch, an inductor, and an output capacitor to produce an output voltage lower than the input by PWM control of the duty cycle.

Buck converter output Vout ~= Vin * duty for an ideal converter; the controller regulates by measuring Vout through a feedback divider and adjusting the duty cycle. A wrong feedback ratio or open feedback pin drives the output off target.
Buck converters require an enable signal and a valid input supply; if EN is held low (by the EC, by UVLO, or by a protection fault) the converter makes no output even if Vin is present.
A boost (step-up) converter charges an inductor from the input and dumps its stored energy through a diode (or synchronous switch) to the output, producing Vout > Vin.
A buck-boost converter can produce a regulated output either above or below the input; it is used where the input range crosses the desired output, e.g. USB-C PD systems and battery-powered rails.

A PWM controller IC drives the power MOSFET(s) with variable duty cycle and fixed frequency; it includes error amplifier, oscillator, slope compensation, current-sense, and protection. The exact pinout, thresholds and register set are component-specific and must come from the datasheet.

A feedback network is a resistor (sometimes capacitor-complexed) divider from the output rail to the feedback pin of the controller; the controller adjusts switching to keep the FB pin at its internal reference (often 0.6-0.8 V).

An open or wrong feedback resistor typically drives the output high (loss of regulation) or causes the controller to stop switching; a shorted FB-to-ground resistor pulls the output down or prevents startup.
UVLO (under-voltage lockout) holds the controller off until Vin exceeds an internal threshold; it prevents malfunction at low input. Threshold values are component-specific.
OVP (over-voltage protection) shuts the converter down if the output rises above a safe limit; it usually indicates loss of regulation and can latch the controller off until input or EN is cycled.

OCP (over-current protection) limits output current via the sense resistor; SCP (short-circuit protection) is a faster, lower-threshold version that triggers on a hard output short. Both can latch the converter off.
Thermal shutdown disables the controller if its die exceeds a threshold; a board that runs briefly then stops may be entering thermal or OCP/SCP latch, not necessarily a permanent fault.

Current is sensed via a small series sense resistor (often 5-20 mOhm on main rails) whose voltage drop is read by the controller; a sense resistor that has been replaced with the wrong value changes the current limit and the regulation behavior.
